person.name: Douglas_Engelbart
person.summary: Douglas Engelbart developed interactive computing tools to help people work together on complex problems. At SRI International, he led the team behind NLS, the computer mouse, hypertext tools, and a famous 1968 demonstration of networked computing.

conclusion: Douglas Engelbart's computer mouse became a standard pointing device for graphical computer interfaces. NLS brought linked documents, screen editing, shared work, and remote collaboration into one working system. The Bootstrap Institute, later the Doug Engelbart Institute, continued to promote his vision for improving collective problem solving.

events.title: Birth in Portland
events.description: Douglas Carl Engelbart was born in Portland, Oregon, to Carl Louis Engelbart and Gladys Charlotte Amelia Munson Engelbart. He grew up between his older sister Dorianne and his younger brother David.

events.title: Serves in the Philippines
events.description: Douglas Engelbart served in the United States Navy as a radio and radar technician in the Philippines. On Leyte, he read Vannevar Bush's [[As We May Think]] and began considering computers as tools for organizing knowledge.

images.caption: U.S. forces land on Leyte, Philippines, 1944
images.creator: Signal Corps Archive from United States

As We May Think.explanation: Vannevar Bush's 1945 essay called for new ways to make knowledge easier to find and use after the war.

events.background:
During World War II, Vannevar Bush directed the U.S. Office of Scientific Research and Development. The office coordinated the wartime work of about 6,000 leading American scientists. Its programs included radar research and the early administration of the Manhattan Project. Bush had begun as an electrical engineer at MIT. In 1927, he started building a differential analyzer. The mechanical analog computer could solve differential equations with as many as 18 independent variables. His proposed memex was an adjustable microfilm viewer. It was designed for a reader to follow and create associative trails among stored materials.

The supplied biography places Engelbart’s Navy service midway through his undergraduate years at Oregon State University. It says that he served for two years. It describes his quarters on Leyte as a small traditional hut on stilts. The article on The Mother of All Demos dates his reading of Bush’s essay to 1946. The biography does not give a more precise year for the reading. Bush published As We May Think in The Atlantic in 1945, as the war was ending.

Bush’s wartime position put him at the center of an enormous expansion of government-supported research. In Science, The Endless Frontier, his 1945 report to the president, he urged continuing federal support for science after the war. He also pressed for the institution that became the National Science Foundation. The later account of Engelbart’s work connects Bush’s essay to a concern about managing the scientific knowledge generated during the war. It says Engelbart came to believe that calculation was only one possible use for computers. He pursued systems for communication and finding information throughout his later research career.

events.title: Earns Engineering Degree
events.description: Douglas Engelbart completed a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at Oregon State University in Corvallis, Oregon, in 1948. He returned to the university after his Navy service to finish his undergraduate studies.

events.title: Defines a Life Mission
events.description: While engaged to Ballard Fish, Douglas Engelbart considered the kind of life and work he wanted. He chose to focus his career on improving how people use their collective intellect to solve serious problems.

events.title: Marries Ballard Fish
events.description: On May 5, 1951, Douglas Engelbart married Ballard Fish at Portola State Park in California. They had met at the Ames Research Center, where Engelbart worked and Fish was completing her training as an occupational therapist.
events.background:
Engelbart had returned to Oregon State University after two years in the Navy as a radio and radar technician in the Philippines. He completed an electrical-engineering degree in 1948. The National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics then hired him at Ames Research Center in northern California. His work there involved wind-tunnel maintenance. In his time away from work, he went hiking and camping and took part in folk dancing. The California period followed a wartime posting on Leyte, where he had read Vannevar Bush’s As We May Think. Bush’s article urged new ways of making knowledge available. It stayed with Engelbart as he considered what kind of work could help people address large problems.

The park setting belonged to a period when his plans were already turning toward graduate study. He had decided in late 1950 that he wanted his career to improve the ability of groups to think and work on difficult questions. Soon afterward, he left Ames for the University of California, Berkeley. He studied electrical engineering with a specialty in computers. Berkeley awarded him a master’s degree in 1953 and a doctorate in 1955.

His doctoral work at Berkeley led to eight patents. He stayed for a year as an assistant professor after completing the doctorate. He then formed Digital Techniques to commercialize storage-device research from his doctoral work. The company lasted a year. He chose to leave it to pursue the research program he had been considering since 1951.

events.title: Completes Doctorate Research
events.description: Douglas Engelbart completed his doctorate in electrical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1955. He remained an assistant professor until 1956, then formed Digital Techniques, a company developing storage devices from his research.

events.title: Joins Stanford Research Institute
events.description: Douglas Engelbart joined Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California, in 1957. He worked with Hewitt Crane on magnetic devices and electronics miniaturization while beginning research on [[interactive computing]].

interactive computing.explanation: Interactive computing lets a person work directly with information on a computer instead of submitting jobs for later processing.

events.title: Publishes Augmentation Framework
events.description: Douglas Engelbart published Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework at Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California, in October 1962. The report proposed computer workstations for organizing and sharing information. It helped secure funding from the Advanced Research Projects Agency for his research program.

event_class.title: Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework
event_class.impact: The report helped secure Advanced Research Projects Agency funding for Engelbart's research program.

events.title: Creates the Computer Mouse
events.description: In 1963, Douglas Engelbart developed the computer mouse at the Augmentation Research Center, his laboratory at Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California. Lead engineer Bill English built the initial prototype from Engelbart’s notes and was its first user.

images.caption: Douglas Engelbart's first computer mouse prototype
images.creator: Michael Hicks from Saint Paul, MN, USA

event_class.title: Computer mouse
event_class.description: A handheld wooden device uses two perpendicular metal wheels to translate motion across a tabletop into X and Y cursor coordinates.
event_class.impact: The mouse became a standard pointing device for graphical computer interfaces.

events.title: Demonstrates NLS in San Francisco
events.description: Douglas Engelbart presented the oN-Line System, or NLS, at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco on December 9, 1968. Bill English directed the technical production while Jeff Rulifson, Bill Paxton, and other ARC researchers joined from Menlo Park. Engelbart used a mouse to edit text, follow [[hypertext]] links, resize windows, and work with the remote team through live audio and video connections.

images.caption: Douglas Engelbart practices the 1968 Mother of All Demos
images.creator: SRI International

hypertext.explanation: Hypertext connects pieces of information so a reader can move directly from one item to related material.

events.background:
The Augmentation Research Center had spent six years assembling NLS with support from NASA and the Advanced Research Projects Agency. At the urging of ARPA director Robert Taylor, the system made its first public appearance at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. The session carried the formal title “A research center for augmenting human intellect.” About 1,000 computer professionals filled San Francisco’s Civic Auditorium. Alan Kay, Charles Irby, Andy van Dam, and Bob Sproull were among those in the audience. Most computing at the time centered on large machines whose users submitted work through intermediaries or shared terminals.

The presentation depended on an elaborate connection between the auditorium and ARC’s Menlo Park laboratory. Two homemade 1,200-baud modems carried data over a leased telephone line between the stage terminal and an SDS 940 computer at SRI. A baud measures the rate at which signals are sent. Two microwave links carried the live two-way video. An Eidophor projector put the computer’s output on a screen 22 feet high. Bill English operated a video switcher to select the image seen by the audience. Stewart Brand ran a camera at the Menlo Park end. Brand was then known as editor of the Whole Earth Catalog.

NLS had been built around shared work on documents, and the remote portions of the presentation made that arrangement visible. Rulifson had written the NLS command language, its first online editor, and the files used for the program. He also redesigned the system’s file structure. Paxton and Rulifson appeared in a separate area of the projected image at different points. They could see one another’s screen, talk, and edit the same text from ARC. The session lasted 90 minutes. The audience gave Engelbart a standing ovation. A separate room afterward let conference attendees inspect NLS workstations and ask questions. Similar projects followed at Xerox PARC in the early 1970s, and NLS concepts later influenced the interfaces of Apple Macintosh and Microsoft Windows.

events.title: Moves NLS to Tymshare
events.description: SRI management placed the remaining ARC staff under Bertram Raphael in 1976. Raphael negotiated the transfer of ARC and its NLS software to Tymshare, a computing services company. Engelbart joined Tymshare as a senior scientist, and the company renamed NLS Augment.
events.background:
Federal support for ARC had been shrinking for several years before 1976. The 1969 Mansfield Amendment ended military financing for research without a military purpose. The end of the Vietnam War and the Apollo program further reduced money from ARPA and NASA during the early 1970s. ARC had relied on those agencies for its work. SRI management also disapproved of Engelbart’s way of running the center.

The laboratory had lost several key researchers by the early 1970s. Some went to Xerox PARC, including researchers who wanted to pursue personal computers. Engelbart continued to favor networked time-sharing systems. In a time-sharing system, many people used terminals connected to one large computer. The disagreement joined a broader conflict over centralized computing. Many younger programmers distrusted centralized power. The rise of personal computing gave that view a technical direction.

ARC’s internal cohesion also suffered from social experiments. Beginning in 1972, several staff members participated in Erhard Seminars Training, known as EST. Engelbart later served for years on EST’s board of directors. The controversial program lowered morale in the lab. During the same period, Engelbart’s house in Atherton burned down, adding strain on his family.

Tymshare already knew the system through a joint project with ARC. It had run a local copy of NLS on a minicomputer called OFFICE-1. Its Office Automation Division offered the renamed system as a commercial service. Operational demands soon took priority over further research. Executives at Tymshare expressed interest in Engelbart’s ideas. They did not commit the money or staff needed to continue developing them.

events.title: Leaves McDonnell Douglas
events.description: McDonnell Douglas acquired Tymshare in 1984. Douglas Engelbart retired from McDonnell Douglas in 1986 after the company did not provide the funding and staff to develop his ideas.

events.title: Launches Bootstrap Institute
events.description: Douglas Engelbart and his daughter Christina Engelbart founded the Bootstrap Institute in 1988. The organization promoted his vision for improving collective problem solving, especially at Stanford University.
events.background:
After retiring from McDonnell Douglas in 1986, Engelbart wanted to continue the work without the commercial pressure that had limited research on his ideas. The new institute turned those ideas into management seminars at Stanford University. From 1989 through 2000, it offered three-day and half-day sessions for people responsible for organizations and their information systems. The sessions treated computers as part of a larger effort to improve how groups handle knowledge and solve difficult problems.

Engelbart called the aim Collective IQ. He used the term for an organization's ability to work together on important problems. His method was a strategic bootstrapping approach. The people seeking better ways to collaborate would also improve the tools and working methods used in that effort. The institute’s seminar graduates formed the Bootstrap Alliance in the early 1990s. The nonprofit alliance became a base for collaborative attempts to put those ideas into practice.

The alliance faced cutbacks when the invasion of Iraq and a subsequent recession led its partner organizations to reorganize and redirect their work. Management seminars, consulting, and small collaborations continued. In the mid-1990s, DARPA funded work on Visual AugTerm, a modern user interface for Augment. The project took part in a larger program studying the information-technology needs of the Joint Task Force. In 2005, a National Science Foundation grant supported the open-source HyperScope project. Its team built a browser component with Ajax and Dynamic HTML to reproduce Augment’s ability to present multiple views and jump within and between documents.

events.title: Receives Turing Award
events.description: The Association for Computing Machinery awarded Douglas Engelbart the A. M. Turing Award in 1997. The award recognized his contributions to human-computer interaction, including the mouse, hypertext, and networked computers.

Association for Computing Machinery.explanation: The Association for Computing Machinery is an international professional society for computing researchers and practitioners.

events.title: Receives National Medal
events.description: President Bill Clinton awarded Douglas Engelbart the [[National Medal of Technology]] in Washington, D.C., in December 2000. The award recognized Engelbart's contributions to human-computer interaction.

National Medal of Technology.explanation: This United States honor recognizes people and organizations whose work has advanced technology and technological innovation.

events.title: Death in Atherton
events.description: Douglas Engelbart was diagnosed with [[Alzheimer's disease]] in 2007. He lived at home in Atherton, California, with his second wife, Karen O'Leary Engelbart. He died there from kidney failure on July 2, 2013, at age 88.

Alzheimer's disease.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive brain disorder that impairs memory and other cognitive abilities.
